A.q: What should the first slide of a presentation typically include?
options: The title of the presentation alone, with no mention of the presenter's name, position, or affiliation
Title, your name, position, affiliation, and optionally additional information such as date or institution logo
The detailed body content of the presentation, omitting the title, the presenter's name, and the affiliation
A.explain: Cover slide: title plus name, position, affiliation (with optional date or institution logo), not detailed content.

A.q: Which of the following combinations is considered most readable for text?
options: Light font on a light background (e.g., yellow on white)
Dark font on a light background (e.g., blue on white)
Dark font on a dark background (e.g., black on navy)
A.explain: Dark font on light background gives the strongest, most readable contrast.

A.q: Which of the following is a recommended way to end a presentation effectively?
options: Stop speaking abruptly the instant your allotted time runs out, with no summary or closing remark
End with a strong closing slide that summarizes the key take-home messages for the audience to remember
Repeat the cover slide verbatim as the final screen so the talk closes on the title and name
A.explain: End with a strong closing summarizing the key take-home messages; never end abruptly.

A.q: Which statement best defines a presentation?
options: A written examination paper that a student submits to the instructor for grading and marks
An informal, unstructured chat between two classmates recalling what was said in a previous lecture
A process of communicating knowledge, thoughts, ideas, and/or research results to specific audiences
A printed handout of reference notes photocopied and distributed to the class after the session ends
A.explain: A presentation communicates knowledge, thoughts, ideas, and/or research results to specific audiences.

A.q: The 'presentation circuit' consists of which four components?
options: Presenter, audience, message, and the setting or context surrounding them
Slides, projector, podium, and the microphone or sound system in the room
Title, outline, body, and the list of references at the end
Writer, editor, reviewer, and the publisher who prints the final copy
A.explain: Presenter and audience around a message, all inside a setting or context.

A.q: Which academic tasks require the ability to write papers scientifically and professionally?
options: Multiple-choice examinations, attendance registers, and oral quizzes
Assignments, research activities, scientific reports, and dissertations
Social media posts, personal text messages, and casual chat
Reading textbooks, listening to lectures, and watching videos
A.explain: Assignments, research activities, scientific reports, and dissertations require scientific and professional writing.

A.q: A successful person is described as one who is capable of:
options: Standing and speaking continuously without a pause or break for a full hour on end
Memorizing the exact wording of each slide and reciting it back word for word
Deliberately avoiding the audience's eyes and reading from the notes held in the hand
Communicating his knowledge, experiences, and thoughts in a professional manner
A.explain: A successful person communicates knowledge, experiences, and thoughts in a professional manner.

A.q: What are the 3 P's of presentation?
options: Plan, Prepare, Present
Practice, Perform, Publish
Plan, Print, Prove
Prepare, Pause, Perfect
A.explain: The 3 P's are Plan, Prepare, Present.

A.q: The reminder 'A person who is going nowhere normally gets there' is attached to which planning step?
options: Locating the suitable resources
Collecting ideas and information
Setting your goal
Designing the background colors
A.explain: It is paired with the step of setting your goal.

A.q: Which set of actions belongs to the PLAN stage?
options: Choosing the font, checking the spelling, designing the background, and thanking the audience at the end
Setting your goal, collecting ideas and information, locating suitable resources, and knowing your audience beforehand
Scanning the audience's eyes, diversifying the voice, synchronizing the hands, and smiling at the questioner
Handling nasty questions with humor, managing the time, hiding the accent, and thanking the audience
A.explain: Plan covers goal, ideas, resources, and knowing your audience beforehand.

A.q: In the three-part organization, 'Tell them what you told them' is which part?
options: The opening
The message
The closing
The cover slide
A.explain: The closing tells them what you told them.

A.q: What should the OPENING of your talk do, according to the organization rule?
options: Tell them what you are going to say
Tell the audience what you told them earlier
Invite the audience to pose nasty questions now
Show the audience the conclusion graph up front
A.explain: The opening tells them what you are going to say.

A.q: The first slide of a presentation must contain:
options: The complete verbatim text of the whole talk, written out in full paragraphs on one screen
The title of the presentation and your name, position, and affiliation
The organization or institution logo alone, with no title, name, or affiliation shown
The full list of references and citations used, placed alone on the opening screen
A.explain: Title plus name, position, and affiliation (with optional date or institution logo).

A.q: Your second slide should list:
options: Every reference and citation written out in full on the slide
The closing thank-you message addressed to the audience and organizers
Complete paragraphs reproducing the introduction of the paper word for word
The objectives, agenda, or outline of your talk, main points only
A.explain: Objectives or agenda, main points only; follow that order for the rest of the talk.

A.q: The recommended slide count is:
options: 1–2 slides per minute of your presentation
Just 1 or 2 slides in total for the whole presentation, regardless of its length
Around 10 slides for each minute of your scheduled presentation time
As many slides as the presentation file can physically hold on the computer screen
A.explain: Use 1–2 slides per minute.

A.q: Good slide structure means writing:
options: Complete, grammatically full sentences packed with as many descriptive words as possible
Full paragraphs copied word for word straight from the textbook onto the screen
In point form, key words and phrases only, 4–5 points per slide
At least twelve separate bullet points crammed onto each prepared slide
A.explain: Point form, 4–5 points per slide, key words only; avoid wordiness.

A.q: Why is showing one point at a time recommended?
options: It significantly reduces the overall file size of the presentation stored on the computer
It helps the audience concentrate, prevents them from reading ahead, and keeps your talk focused
It quietly hides your weakest arguments and least-prepared points from the watching audience
It is a compulsory feature built into most presentation software programs
A.explain: It helps concentration, prevents reading ahead, and keeps the talk focused.

A.q: Which rule matches the advice on animation?
options: Apply a different noisy animation to each slide, layer several effects, and change the style often
Load the deck with as much animation as possible, since more motion keeps the audience alert
Do not use distracting animation, avoid noisy effects, do not go overboard, and be consistent
Leave animation out and depend on static cuts, believing motion hurts focus
A.explain: No distracting or noisy animation, do not overdo it, and be consistent.

A.q: Using the Verdana font, content text should be no smaller than what size?
options: 12 point
24 point
32 point
40 point
A.explain: Title about 40 pt, bullets about 32 pt, content no smaller than 24 pt.

A.q: Which fonts are named as standard, readable choices for slides?
options: Garamond, Century Gothic, Gill Sans, and Times
Times New Roman, Tahoma, Verdana, or Arial
Garamond Italic, Gill Sans Condensed, Century Gothic, and Times Bold
Verdana, Tahoma, Gill Sans, and Century Gothic
A.explain: Times New Roman, Tahoma, Verdana, or Arial are the standard readable choices.

A.q: Why should you NOT use all capital letters?
options: The presentation software simply refuses to display text written in capital letters
Typing in capitals automatically shortens the total running time of the presentation
It makes text hard to read, conceals acronyms, and denies capitals for EMPHASIS
Using capitals affects the footer line but leaves the body of the slide unchanged
A.explain: ALL CAPS is hard to read, conceals acronyms, and denies capitals for emphasis.

A.q: Italics are properly used for:
options: Italicize each bullet point on the slide so the list stands out
Quotes, highlighting thoughts or ideas, and titles of books, journals, or magazines
Apply italics to the headings and titles rather than to ordinary body text
Use italics for numbers and statistics rather than for ordinary words or phrases
A.explain: Quotes, highlighted thoughts or ideas, and book, journal, or magazine titles.

A.q: Which rule governs font color?
options: Assign a brand-new, different color to each individual point or even each word
Place bright, vivid colors directly on a plain white background for maximum pop
Choose a font color that matches the background color exactly, blending them together
Use a font color that contrasts sharply with the background
A.explain: Contrast sharply with the background: dark font on light background.

A.q: What is advised about presentation backgrounds?
options: Use light backgrounds and keep the same background consistently throughout
Choose dark, cluttered, busy backgrounds in order to add drama and intensity to the talk
Switch to a brand-new background on each slide to keep the audience alert
Believe that the choice of background has little effect on how readable the text is
A.explain: Light backgrounds, the same background consistently throughout.

A.q: Which set of combinations appears on the 'avoid such combinations' list?
options: White on black, dark yellow on green, purple on blue, orange on green, red on green
Green on blue, dark yellow on green, blue on white, orange on green, red on green
Green on blue, dark yellow on green, purple on blue, orange on green, red on green
Green on blue, dark yellow on green, purple on blue, orange on green, dark text on a light background
A.explain: Avoid green on blue, dark yellow on green, purple on blue, orange on green, and red on green, plus bright colors on white.

A.q: Why are graphs recommended rather than just tables and words?
options: Drawing a graph simply takes far less time than typing out the equivalent table
Data in graphs is easier to comprehend and retain, and trends are easier to visualize
A graph is allowed to skip its title because the axes explain the data on their own
Tables are discouraged and should not appear in a scientific presentation
A.explain: Data in graphs is easier to comprehend and retain, and trends are easier to visualize; title every graph.

A.q: In the faulty-graph example, which faults were called out?
options: Minor gridlines unnecessary, font too small, colors illogical, title missing, shading distracting
Too few colors used, dull monochrome look, line plots instead of bars, months mislabeled, legend absent
Graph drawn too small, axes reversed, bold gridlines, over-long title, missing shading
Bars used instead of lines, colors too logical, font too large, no shading, title present
A.explain: Unnecessary gridlines, too-small font, illogical colors, missing title, and distracting shading.

A.q: About spelling and syntax, you are advised to:
options: Rely on the audience to silently correct the spelling mistakes you leave on the screen
Bother to check the spelling after the presentation is over and the audience gone
Proofread your presentation before they see it, and asking a friend for help is OK
Ignore spelling, on the theory that the content is what really matters
A.explain: Proofread before they see it; asking a friend for help is OK.

A.q: Why is an effective and strong closing important?
options: It reduces the total number of slides you show
Your audience is likely to remember your last words
It prevents the audience from asking more questions
It replaces the outline slide at the very end
A.explain: The audience is likely to remember your last words: take-home messages, no abrupt ending.

A.q: What is the purpose of the 'Questions' slide at the end of a presentation?
options: Use the final screen to invite your audience to step forward and ask questions
Use the final screen to read out the complete list of references and citations
Use the final screen to display the title and your name one more time
Use the final screen to announce the topic and date of the next lecture
A.explain: Invite your audience to ask questions and handle them well.

A.q: 'The mind starts working the minute you're born, and never stops until you get up to speak' humorously refers to:
options: Audience boredom
Writer's block during essays
Presentation phobia
Time management failure
A.explain: Presentation phobia, which can be healthy or unhealthy.

A.q: Complete the key sentence about delivery: 'It is not WHAT we say, but…'
options: how long we speak
HOW we say it
how many slides we show
how loudly we apologize
A.explain: It is not WHAT we say, but HOW we say it.

A.q: Which treatment is given for presentation phobia?
options: Practice using colleagues, friends, or relatives as audiences, and breathe deeply before you stand
Avoid giving presentations for a full year, hoping the fear fades on its own
Rehearse the talk only in front of mirrors, steering clear of any live audience
Read every slide aloud word-for-word throughout the talk so that no mistake slips through
A.explain: Practice repeatedly with friendly audiences, and take a couple of deep breaths before standing up.

A.q: Match each tip number to the advice it gives.

rightItems.text: Get well dressed and arrive early to the stage
Introduce yourself, as people buy people first
Start a two-way conversation fed back by body language
Scan the audience's eyes on a regular basis

A.explain: Tip 1 is dressing and arriving early, tip 2 introducing yourself, tip 3 commencing a two-way conversation, tip 4 scanning the audience's eyes.

A.q: Match each tip number to the advice it gives.

rightItems.text: Behave naturally rather than stiffly or rehearsed
Synchronize your gestures with your words
Do not roam to and fro, which distracts listeners
Diversify tone between loud, soft, fast and slow

A.explain: Tip 5 is being natural, tip 6 synchronizing hand movements with words, tip 7 limiting body movement, tip 8 diversifying the voice.

A.q: Match each tip number to the advice it gives.

rightItems.text: Use a deliberate pause as a positive sound effect
Drop self-importance and apologies that devalue the talk
Skip hard technical terms unless you explain them
Let listeners discover gaps instead of being told

A.explain: Tip 9 is using silence well, tip 10 avoiding bad habits, tip 11 explaining jargon, tip 12 letting the audience discover rather than be told.

A.q: Match each tip number to the advice it gives.

rightItems.text: Keep to your allotted time and do not overrun
Do not artificially mask the way you naturally sound
Repeat unclear questions; if stumped, apologize with humor
Smile, approach the questioner, defer or bounce it back

A.explain: Tip 13 is time management, tip 14 not hiding your accent, tip 15 handling questions well, tip 16 handling nasty questions.

A.q: Match each tip number to the advice it gives.

rightItems.text: Face audience, do not block projection, know what is behind
Use humor but do not overuse it
Hold attention and avoid boring the audience
Close by thanking the audience at the end

A.explain: Tip 17 is posture, tip 18 using humor in moderation, tip 19 maintaining attention, tip 20 thanking the audience.

A.q: The Verdana font sizes form a descending ladder for slides.

steps.prompt: What size does the ladder give a title?
options: 40 point
32 point
24 point
12 point

steps.prompt: Below the 40-point title, what size is for subtitles or bullets?
options: 32 point
24 point
12 point
40 point

steps.prompt: Below the 32-point bullets, content must be no smaller than what?
options: 24 point
12 point
32 point
40 point

steps.prompt: The smallest rung, not recommended for content, is what size?
options: 12 point
24 point
32 point
40 point

A.explain: Titles 40 pt, subtitles or bullets 32 pt, content no smaller than 24 pt, and 12 pt is not recommended for content.

A.q: A finished talk follows a fixed slide order.

steps.prompt: The opening slide is the cover; what must it carry?
options: Title plus name, position and affiliation
The full reference list
The thank-you note
The conclusion graph

steps.prompt: After the cover, the second slide lists what?
options: The objectives or agenda, main points only
Every citation in full
The closing summary
The questions prompt

steps.prompt: The body delivers the message; which slide comes right before Questions?
options: The conclusion summarizing main points
The cover again
The agenda
The title only

steps.prompt: What is the last slide's purpose after the conclusion?
options: Invite the audience to ask questions
Reprint the title
Read references
Announce next topic

A.explain: Cover first with title, name and affiliation, then the agenda of main points, then the message, then a conclusion summarizing points and suggesting future research, and finally a slide inviting questions.

A.q: Which are listed as bad habits that switch off the audience?
options: Claiming to be the top expert in the field
Apologizing for having nothing important or being unprepared
Explaining difficult jargon to the audience
Scanning the audience's eyes on a regular basis
A.explain: Self-importance and apologizing are bad habits that devalue speaker and talk; explaining jargon and scanning eyes are good practices, not bad habits.

A.q: Which does the topic say happens to the body when you are nervous?
options: Blood pressure changes
Adrenaline level increases
You turn red, shake, or perspire
Your voice becomes noticeably deeper
A.explain: Nervousness changes blood pressure, raises adrenaline, and makes you turn red, shake or perspire; a deeper voice is not mentioned.

A.q: Which are valid ways to handle a nasty question?
options: Smile at the person asking
Make eye contact and move toward them
Throw the question back to them
Offer to answer privately afterward
Ignore the questioner and move on
A.explain: Smiling, approaching the questioner, bouncing the question back, or deferring to a private answer are all valid; ignoring the questioner is not advised.

A.q: All of the following are intended outcomes except:
options: Define what a presentation is
Plan and prepare a good presentation
List important tips for presenting
Recite each slide from memory
A.explain: The aims are to define, plan, prepare and list tips for presentations; reciting slides from memory is not one of them.

A.q: Writing and presenting information are highlighted as important skills especially for whom?
options: A medical student and a health professional
Only seasoned researchers and professors
Just administrative and office staff
Exclusively journalists and editors
A.explain: They matter for anyone, but the medical student and the health professional are stressed in particular.

A.q: In what order does the topic say to develop the work?
options: Write, then transform into a presentation, then present
Present, then write the essay, then edit it
Design slides, then write, then plan the talk
Plan the audience, then present, then write
A.explain: Write an essay or assignment first, transform it into a presentation, then present it to the target audience.

A.q: Why is a word-packed paragraph slide considered bad?
options: The audience reads instead of listening to you
It makes the file size grow too large
It hides weak points from the viewers
It forces the speaker to memorize the text
A.explain: A paragraph slide is hard to read and present, so the audience spends time reading rather than listening, even with the same number of points.

A.q: Why is combining a small font with bold or italics discouraged?
options: It makes the text very hard to read
It uses up the slide too quickly
It conflicts with the background color rule
It shortens the running time of the talk
A.explain: Small type already strains readability, and adding bold or italics makes it worse, so the combination is not recommended.

A.q: Where does the topic allow a small font size?
options: In the footer line of a slide
In the main body bullet points
In the title of every slide
In the graph axis labels only
A.explain: Small fonts are acceptable for a footer, such as a date or presenter name, but not for body content.

A.q: What principle do the broken font styles illustrate?
options: Never trade readability for visual style
Always prefer decorative script fonts
Use italics for every heading
Capitalize all text for emphasis
A.explain: The same phrase shown in italic, capitals, script and bold caps all hurt legibility, teaching that readability must not be sacrificed for style.

A.q: Beyond sharp contrast, how should color be used on slides?
options: To reinforce structure and occasionally emphasize
As a fresh color for every single word
Only in the footer and not in body text
To match the background and blend fully
A.explain: Color should reinforce the logic of the structure and emphasize a point only occasionally; a different color per word is discouraged.

A.q: Why are bright colors on a white background a bad mix?
options: They give low contrast and become unreadable
They make the file size too large
They hide the acronyms in the text
They conflict with the animation rule
A.explain: Bright colors on white yield low contrast and are unreadable, unlike a dark font on a light background which reads well.

A.q: What two rules govern graphs and charts?
options: Always title them, and avoid complex ones
Never title them, and prefer complex ones
Use only tables, never graphs or charts
Shade every bar and add minor gridlines
A.explain: Graphs should always carry a title and stay simple; complex graphs and distracting shading or gridlines are discouraged.

A.q: Proofreading a presentation means checking which three things?
options: Spelling, grammar and punctuation
Font, color and background
Title, agenda and references
Voice, posture and humor
A.explain: Before the audience sees it, proofread for spelling, grammar and punctuation, and asking a friend for help is fine.

A.q: A conclusion slide should do which two things?
options: Summarize the main points and suggest future research
Reprint the title and list all references
Invite questions and thank the organizers
Show the agenda and play an animation
A.explain: The conclusion slide summarizes the main points of the talk and suggests future avenues of research.

A.q: Into which two kinds does the topic divide presentation phobia?
options: Healthy phobia and unhealthy phobia
Mild phobia and severe phobia
Stage phobia and camera phobia
Voice phobia and eye phobia
A.explain: Presentation phobia is split into a healthy form and an unhealthy form; the treatment is practice plus deep breaths.

A.q: In the three-part organization, the MESSAGE part does what?
options: Tell them, between the opening and closing
Tell them what you are going to say
Tell them what you already told them
Tell them to prepare the agenda
A.explain: The message is the body that simply tells them, sitting between the opening (what you will say) and the closing (what you told them).

A.q: Which saying is remembered before you speak, prompting you to introduce yourself?
options: People buy people first
Time is money always
Practice makes perfect only
The customer is right
A.explain: Before speaking, introduce yourself, remembering that people buy people first, so the person connects before the content.

A.q: Starting a talk is framed as beginning what, fed back through body language?
options: A two-way conversation
A one-way lecture
A written report
A silent reading
A.explain: You commence a two-way conversation; the audience feeds you back through their body language.

A.q: If you are unsure of a question from the audience, what should you do?
options: Ask for the question to be repeated
Ignore it and continue talking
Apologize profusely and sit down
Make up an answer immediately
A.explain: When uncertain, ask for the question to be repeated; if you lack an answer, apologize with some humor rather than faking one.

A.q: Which posture rule is given for the presenter?
options: Face the audience unless pointing at something
Stand in front of the projection screen
Turn your back to read the slides
Pace to and fro across the whole stage
A.explain: Do not block the projection, always face the audience unless pointing, and know what is behind you without looking.

A.q: What is the advice about using humor in a presentation?
options: Use it, but do not overuse it
Leave humor out and stay serious throughout
Add humor to most of your points
Use humor solely when answering nasty questions
A.explain: A sense of humor helps, but it should be used in moderation and not overdone.

A.q: How should a presenter handle what the audience does not know?
options: Let them discover it, rather than being told
Tell them plainly that they lack the knowledge
Ignore the gap and move to the next slide
Apologize for the missing background information
A.explain: Do not tell the audience they do not know; let them discover it themselves, which avoids putting them down.

A.q: Which tip is matched correctly to its advice?
options: Hand Movements: synchronize gestures with your words
Body Movements: synchronize gestures with your words
Voice: treat a deliberate pause as a positive effect
Silence: vary loudness, softness, speed and pace
A.explain: Hand movements means syncing gestures with words, while body movements means not roaming; voice means varying tone, and silence means using a pause well.

A.q: Writing a good paper is described as having how many steps?
options: Ten
Three
Five
Twenty
A.explain: The stated count is ten steps for writing a good paper; three, five and twenty are not given.
